title: From Labs to Living Rooms
summary: In the 1980s, people at home began plugging their computers into the phone line. Modems screeched, message boards buzzed and a speedy new science network called NSFNET grew into the Internet's main highway. By 1995 the Internet was open to everyone, not just scientists.

sections.heading: Squeals, Hisses and Bits Per Second
paragraphs: Imagine it is a rainy evening in 1993. You switch on the family computer, click an icon, and from a little box beside it comes the strangest noise: a dial tone, a quick burst of beeps as a phone number is dialled, then a long, high whistle, followed by crunching, hissing and warbling like two robots arguing inside a seashell. After about twenty seconds the noise stops. You are online.

That noisy box was a modem. The word is short for modulator-demodulator. Telephone lines were built to carry human voices, which are wobbly sound waves, not the neat 1s and 0s that computers use. So a modem 'modulates' bits into sounds, sends the sounds down the phone line, and the modem at the other end 'demodulates' the sounds back into bits. In a way, two modems really were singing to each other.

The screeching had a purpose. It was the 'handshake', a short conversation in which the two modems tested the line. One tone told the telephone network to switch off its echo-cancelling equipment, which would otherwise mess up the data. Then the modems sent test signals back and forth to measure how noisy the line was, and agreed on the fastest speed it could safely handle. A crackly line meant a slower connection.

Modem speeds were measured in bits per second. One of the first popular modems for data, AT&T's Bell 103 from 1962, ran at 300 bits per second. Early home users sometimes used an 'acoustic coupler', a box with two rubber cups that gripped an ordinary telephone handset, so the computer literally whistled into the mouthpiece. In 1981 the Hayes Smartmodem, also at 300 bits per second, became a hit because a computer could control it with simple text commands, many of which started with the letters AT. Those 'AT commands' are still built into some modems today.

Over the next fifteen years speeds climbed: 1,200, then 2,400, then 9,600 bits per second, then 14,400 and 28,800 in the early and mid-1990s. The last big step was 56 kilobits per second, standardised in 1998. Even then, 56k modems rarely reached their top speed. Most homes got something more like 40 to 50 kilobits per second in the download direction, and uploads were slower still.

Let us do some maths to feel how slow that was. A single holiday photo from a modern phone might be about 3 megabytes, which is about 24 million bits. At 56,000 bits per second, even in perfect conditions, that one picture would take about seven minutes to arrive. At 2,400 bits per second it would take nearly three hours. Today a home fibre connection can fetch the same photo in a fraction of a second.

Dial-up had another catch. Because the modem used the phone line, nobody else in the house could make or receive a call while you were online. Remember the big idea from Part 1: a phone call ties up a whole circuit for as long as it lasts. Dial-up Internet was packet switching riding on top of an old circuit-switched phone call. In many countries, including Britain, phone calls were charged by the minute, so parents watched the clock, and some families saved their Internet time for evenings and weekends when calls were cheaper.

sections.heading: Bulletin Boards and the Great Usenet Conversation
paragraphs: Long before most families had heard of the Internet, hobbyists with modems were already chatting to strangers. In January and February 1978 a huge blizzard buried Chicago in snow. Stuck indoors, two computer club members, Ward Christensen and Randy Suess, built a program that let people phone up a computer and leave messages for each other, like pinning notes on a cork board. They called it CBBS, the Computerized Bulletin Board System, and it went online in February 1978.

The idea spread fast. A bulletin board system, or BBS, was usually one personal computer in someone's spare room or basement, attached to one phone line. The owner was called the 'sysop', short for system operator. Because there was only one line, only one person could be connected at a time, so popular boards were often busy and you had to keep redialling. Once connected, you could read and post messages, play simple text games and download small programs and files.

Most boards were local, because long-distance calls were expensive. So in 1984 a programmer in San Francisco, Tom Jennings, created FidoNet. Late at night, during a special 'mail hour' when calls were cheaper, FidoNet boards phoned each other and passed on bundles of messages, like a relay of postal vans moving mail from town to town. By the early 1990s there were tens of thousands of bulletin boards in the United States alone.

Meanwhile, at universities, a different conversation was beginning. In 1979 two graduate students at Duke University in North Carolina, Tom Truscott and Jim Ellis, wanted a way for computer users at different universities to share news and discussions. They worked with Steve Bellovin, a student at the nearby University of North Carolina, who wrote the first version of the software. In 1980 their system, called Usenet, linked Duke and UNC, and it soon spread to other campuses.

Usenet did not need the ARPANET. It ran on the Unix operating system, which AT&T had spread widely to universities, and it used a Unix program called UUCP to make computers phone each other, often at night, and swap new articles. Each computer kept a copy of the latest messages and passed them on to its neighbours, so a post written in North Carolina could gradually spread across the country and then the world. Some people called Usenet 'the poor man's ARPANET', because any university with a Unix computer and a modem could join.

Usenet messages were sorted into 'newsgroups', each about one topic. In 1987 the groups were reorganised into big families with names like comp (computers), sci (science), rec (hobbies and recreation), soc (society) and talk, and soon an 'alt' family for alternative topics appeared too. A group name read like an address: rec.arts.books, or sci.space. Thousands of groups grew, on everything from astronomy to cooking.

Usenet is where many online habits were born. Long-running groups wrote lists of frequently asked questions, or FAQs, so newcomers would not ask the same thing over and over. Usenet also became the place to announce big new ideas. In 1991 a Finnish student named Linus Torvalds announced his new operating system, later called Linux, on a Usenet group, and as you will discover in Part 10, the World Wide Web was announced on Usenet too.

sections.heading: Walled Gardens: CompuServe, Prodigy, AOL and Minitel
paragraphs: Most families who went online in the 1980s and early 1990s did not actually connect to the Internet at all. Instead, they joined an 'online service', a big company that ran its own private network. You paid a monthly fee, dialled the company's local phone number, and stepped into its own world of news, games, shopping, email and chat rooms. People later called these services 'walled gardens': pleasant and well kept, but with high walls around them.

CompuServe, based in Columbus, Ohio, started in 1969 as a business that rented time on its big computers. In 1979 it began offering a service for home computer owners, and in 1980 it launched the CB Simulator, one of the first public online chat systems, named after the citizens band radios that truck drivers used. CompuServe members had email addresses made of numbers with a comma in the middle. In 1987 a CompuServe engineer, Steve Wilhite, created the GIF image format, which is still used for short looping animations today.

Prodigy, launched across the United States in 1990 by IBM and the department store company Sears, tried to make going online colourful. Its screens had simple pictures and a strip of advertising along the bottom, and it charged a flat monthly price. Then came America Online, or AOL. It grew out of a small company called Quantum Computer Services, which in 1985 launched Q-Link, a service for owners of the Commodore 64 home computer. Renamed America Online in 1991, it became famous for mailing out free trial discs, first floppy disks and later CDs, by the millions. Opening one meant hearing a cheerful recorded voice announce: 'You've got mail!'

Across the Atlantic, France had built something even bigger. Starting with trials in 1980 and a national launch from 1982, the French telephone service rolled out Minitel. Instead of printing huge paper phone books, it gave families a small terminal for free: a beige box with a little screen and a fold-down keyboard that plugged into the phone line. At first people used it to look up phone numbers, but soon they were buying train tickets, checking bank accounts, reading the news, checking exam results and chatting.

Minitel had a clever way of paying for things. Services had short codes such as 3615 followed by a name, and the cost appeared on the family's normal phone bill, charged by the minute. The phone company shared the money with the companies that ran the services, which encouraged thousands of them to appear. Millions of French homes had a Minitel terminal, years before most of the world had seen a web page. It kept running until it was finally switched off on 30 June 2012.

Here is the important point: Minitel was not the Internet. It was a central, national system run by one organisation, built on its own rules, and it did not connect freely to other networks. CompuServe, Prodigy and AOL were similar islands. You could only talk to people inside the same garden. What these services proved, though, was that ordinary people, not only scientists, really wanted to be online. They wanted news, shopping, games and, above all, a way to talk to each other. When the walls later came down, those millions of users poured onto the open Internet.

sections.heading: NSFNET: A Faster Highway for Science
paragraphs: While families were dialling up bulletin boards, American scientists had a different problem. In the mid-1980s the US National Science Foundation, or NSF, paid for a handful of new supercomputer centres, packed with some of the fastest computers in the world. Supercomputers were extremely expensive, so only a few could be built. Researchers at hundreds of other universities needed a way to reach them from far away. Does that sound familiar? It was exactly the same reason ARPA had wanted a network back in the 1960s: sharing expensive machines.

In 1985 Dennis Jennings, an Irish computer scientist leading the NSF networking programme, made a decision that shaped the future: every network in the programme would have to use TCP/IP, the same rules as the ARPANET. That meant the new network would not be another island. It would plug straight into the growing Internet.

In 1986 the NSFNET backbone was switched on. A 'backbone' is the main set of high-speed links that carries traffic between big regions, like a motorway between cities. The first NSFNET backbone linked six sites, including supercomputer centres at Princeton, Cornell, the University of Illinois, Pittsburgh and San Diego, with links running at 56 kilobits per second. That is about the same as one late dial-up modem, which shows how much speeds would change in just a few years.

Around the backbone grew 'regional networks', such as NYSERNet in New York State and SURAnet in the south-eastern United States. Universities connected to their regional network, and regional networks connected to the backbone. The NSF also insisted that when a university connected, the link should be available to all qualified users on its campus, not just a few computer scientists. Suddenly students and professors in biology, history and music could use the Internet too.

So many people joined that the network quickly became overloaded. In October 1986 traffic jams became so bad that, on one well-known link between Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory and the University of California, Berkeley, only about 400 yards apart, the speed collapsed from about 32,000 bits per second to about 40. Packets were being lost, resent, lost again and resent again, clogging the lines. The computer scientist Van Jacobson studied the problem and in 1988 published changes to TCP that made computers slow down politely when the network was busy, then speed up again gradually. Versions of these 'congestion control' ideas still keep the Internet from jamming today.

The NSF also upgraded the backbone itself. In 1987 it chose Merit, a network group based at the University of Michigan, working with the companies IBM and MCI, to build a faster one. By 1988 the backbone ran at T1 speed, about 1.5 megabits per second, roughly 28 times faster than before, and that same year countries such as Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Norway and Sweden joined. By 1991 the backbone was upgraded again, to T3 links of about 45 megabits per second.

The numbers grew at an astonishing pace. The Computer History Museum records about 2,000 host computers on the Internet at the end of 1985, more than 10,000 in 1987, about 60,000 in 1988 and over 160,000 by late 1989. By 1992 more than a million computers were connected. Over its life, the NSFNET backbone grew from six sites joined by 56-kilobit links to a coast-to-coast network of 45-megabit links.

And what about the old ARPANET, where it all began? By the late 1980s it was slow and outdated compared with NSFNET, and its sites moved over to the newer networks one by one. In 1989 UCLA held a symposium to celebrate twenty years since the first 'LO', and Vint Cerf even wrote a poem for the occasion. The ARPANET was formally decommissioned in 1990. It had grown from four computers to a network that connected to hundreds of thousands, and then it quietly stepped aside. The Internet it had started simply kept going without it.

sections.heading: Breaking Loops: Radia Perlman's Tree
paragraphs: As networks grew, engineers faced a sneaky problem inside buildings and campuses. Remember Ethernet from Part 5, the way of linking computers in one building? To make an Ethernet network bigger, engineers used devices called bridges, which joined two or more network segments together and passed messages between them.

To be safe, network builders liked to add extra bridges and extra cables, so that if one link broke, another path would still work. But that created loops: paths that went round in a circle. Some messages on Ethernet are 'broadcasts', meant for every computer. When a broadcast reached a loop, each bridge copied it and passed it on, and the copies went round and round, multiplying each time, never stopping. Within seconds a network could be flooded so badly that nothing else could get through. Engineers called this a broadcast storm.

In 1984 Radia Perlman, an engineer at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), was asked to solve the problem, and her solution was published in 1985. She had studied mathematics and computer science at MIT, and the solution she designed is called the spanning-tree protocol. The idea is beautifully simple. First, all the bridges 'vote' to choose one bridge as the root, the one with the lowest identification number. Then every other bridge works out its shortest path to the root. Any extra links that would create a loop are switched into a waiting mode, blocked but ready. The result is a tree shape: every part of the network is connected, but there are no circles.

Here is the clever part. If a cable breaks or a bridge fails, the bridges notice and run the process again, waking up one of the waiting links to heal the network automatically. Nobody needs to rush around with a screwdriver. Her design was turned into an official standard, IEEE 802.1D, and spanning tree and its descendants have helped run Ethernet networks in offices, schools and data centres ever since.

Perlman even wrote a poem about her algorithm, called 'Algorhyme', which begins: 'I think that I shall never see / A graph more lovely than a tree.' It is a playful copy of a famous old poem called 'Trees'. In maths, a 'graph' means a set of points joined by lines, and a 'tree' is a graph with no loops.

Perlman went on to design other important systems, including a routing method called IS-IS that still helps route Internet traffic in big networks, and later TRILL, an improvement on spanning tree. She has been granted more than 100 patents and was inducted into the Internet Hall of Fame in 2014. Some newspapers have called her the 'Mother of the Internet', but she has pushed back on that nickname, pointing out that the Internet was built by many people. That is a very Internet-like thing to say.

sections.heading: The Night the Worm Got Loose
paragraphs: On the evening of 2 November 1988, a program was released onto the Internet from a computer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It had been written by Robert Tappan Morris, a 22-year-old graduate student at Cornell University. His aim, it is usually said, was simply to find out how big the Internet was, not to cause damage. But his program contained a serious mistake, and within hours it was spreading out of control.

The program was a worm: a piece of software that copies itself from computer to computer across a network on its own, without anyone opening a file. To get in, it used weaknesses in common programs. One trick used a hidden testing feature in the email software called sendmail. Another overloaded a program called finger, which people used to look up information about other users, by sending it more data than it expected. A third tried to guess weak passwords, using a list of common words.

Morris had tried to stop the worm from copying itself onto computers it had already infected. But to stop people tricking it, he made it copy itself anyway about one time in seven. That was far too often. Computers became infected again and again, until they were running dozens of copies of the worm at once and slowed to a crawl or stopped working. The worm did not delete files or steal information, but it jammed thousands of machines at universities, research labs and military sites.

About 6,000 computers were hit, roughly one in ten of the 60,000 or so computers then on the Internet. That night, system managers at the University of California, Berkeley, MIT and other places stayed up for hours, pulling the worm apart to understand how it worked and writing fixes. Some sites unplugged from the network completely to protect themselves, which also meant they could not receive the warning messages that explained how to fight it. Within a few days the worm had been cleared out, but the clean-up cost a great deal of time and money. Estimates of the cost varied hugely, from about 100,000 dollars to as much as 10 million dollars.

Morris became the first person convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986. In 1990 he was sentenced to three years of probation, 400 hours of community service and a fine of about 10,000 dollars. He later went on to become a respected professor of computer science at MIT, showing that one serious mistake does not have to define a whole life.

The Morris worm was the Internet's first big wake-up call about security. The early network had been built by a small community of researchers who mostly knew and trusted each other. Now it was huge, and one program could cause chaos across the whole country in a single night. Within weeks, DARPA paid for a new team at the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh: the Computer Emergency Response Team, or CERT. Its job was to act like a fire station for computers, collecting reports of attacks, warning people about weaknesses and helping them fix their systems. Many countries later set up similar teams. You will learn much more about hackers, worms and how to stay safe in Part 17.

sections.heading: Open for Business: 1991 to 1995
paragraphs: There was one big rule standing between the Internet and everyday life. NSFNET had an 'Acceptable Use Policy' that said its backbone was only for research and education. You could not use it to run a business or sell things. But the rule only covered the national backbone, not every local and regional network, and private companies began building their own long-distance networks to carry the traffic that NSFNET would not.

Companies such as UUNET, founded in 1987, and PSINet, founded in 1989, started selling Internet connections to businesses. In 1989 a company in Brookline, Massachusetts, called The World began selling dial-up Internet access to members of the public, and it is often said to be the first to do so. In 1991 several of these commercial providers set up the Commercial Internet Exchange, a place where their networks could meet and swap traffic directly, without sending it over NSFNET at all.

Between 1991 and 1992 the rules were loosened step by step, and in 1992 the US Congress passed a law that allowed NSFNET to carry more commercial traffic. Meanwhile, the walled gardens began opening their gates. In 1993 and 1994 big online services such as Delphi and AOL began giving their members access to Usenet. So many newcomers arrived that Usenet old-timers joked that September 1993 had become an 'Eternal September', because every September, new university students used to arrive and learn the rules, and now the newcomers never stopped coming.

The NSF had always planned for the backbone to stand on its own feet one day, without government money. Instead of running one main highway, it arranged for several 'network access points', places in different parts of the United States where commercial networks could connect to each other. Internet service providers, or ISPs, could now carry traffic from coast to coast on their own lines and hand it over at these meeting points.

On 30 April 1995 the NSFNET backbone was switched off. Hardly anyone outside the networking world noticed, and that was the point: the traffic simply flowed through the new commercial networks instead. The money the NSF saved was given to regional networks so they could buy connections from the private long-distance companies. In about eight and a half years, the backbone had helped the Internet grow to more than 50,000 networks. Now the Internet belonged to no single government or company. It was a giant web of independent networks, all agreeing to use the same open rules.

Think how far things had come since 1979. A few universities swapping messages by phone at night had become millions of people dialling in from their bedrooms and kitchens. But going online was still not easy. You had to know strange commands, remember long computer names and dig through menus of files. Information was scattered across thousands of computers, each organised in its own way.

In fact, one scientist had been grumbling about exactly that problem for years. At CERN, a giant physics laboratory on the border of France and Switzerland, thousands of researchers from all over the world came and went, bringing their own computers, programs and documents. Finding anything was a nightmare. A British physicist and software engineer there was frustrated that useful information kept getting lost in a maze of incompatible machines. His name was Tim Berners-Lee, and he had an idea.

deepDive: Historians often describe the years from about 1985 to 1995 as the moment the Internet changed from a government research project into public infrastructure, and the NSF's choices explain a lot of why it happened so smoothly. Three decisions stand out. First, in 1985 the NSF made TCP/IP compulsory for its networking programme. At the time there were serious rivals, including the international OSI protocols that many governments officially preferred, and private systems from companies like IBM and DEC. By building on TCP/IP, NSFNET joined the existing ARPANET community rather than starting another island, and the sheer growth of NSFNET helped TCP/IP win the so-called protocol wars. Second, the NSF built a hierarchy: a national backbone, regional networks below it, and campus networks below those, while encouraging regionals to find commercial customers. That meant private companies were already involved long before the backbone closed. Third, the Acceptable Use Policy, which banned commercial traffic on the backbone, had an unexpected effect: it pushed businesses such as UUNET and PSINet to build their own long-haul networks, so a commercial Internet existed ready to take over. Not everyone thinks privatisation went perfectly. In 1991 the NSF allowed ANS, a non-profit created by Merit, IBM and MCI to run the backbone, to set up a for-profit arm, and some critics, and a 1992 congressional hearing, questioned whether this gave one group an unfair head start. The fast growth also exposed technical weaknesses. The 1986 congestion collapses showed that TCP needed to react to busy networks, and Van Jacobson's 1988 algorithms, such as slow start, became one of the most important fixes in Internet history. The Morris worm revealed how trusting the old software was. It exploited a buffer overflow in fingerd, where a program writes more data into memory than the space set aside for it, and that kind of bug remained one of the most common security holes for decades. Meanwhile, Perlman's spanning tree shows a theme that runs through the whole story: rather than relying on a central controller, the network's parts follow simple shared rules and organise themselves, and can heal when something breaks.
funFact: France's Minitel network kept running for more than 30 years, from its first trials in 1980 until it was switched off on 30 June 2012, long after most French homes were on the Internet.
